Ringed crayfish Orconectes neglectus inhabits rocky-bottomed streams across the Ozark Plateau, where individuals typically attain an ultimate carapace length of 2.1 centimeters [Li = 2.1 centimeters]. This maximum size is achieved after several molts, with growth decelerating markedly as the asymptotic length is approached. Field surveys of adult populations consistently find the largest individuals measuring at or near this value, suggesting that the species reaches a genuine asymptotic dimension under natural stream conditions. The carapace provides a reliable metric for comparing size across crayfish assemblages, and for Orconectes neglectus the observed maximum is intermediate among its congeners, reflecting a moderate body plan suited to its interstitial and under-rock microhabitats.

The timing of reproductive development in this species is marked by the onset of puberty at a total length of 1.3 centimeters [Lp = 1.3 centimeters], which corresponds to the body dimension at which gonadal maturation begins. Young-of-year crayfish that reach this threshold during their second growing season become capable of mating, though the transition is not abrupt and may span several molts. The total length measured from the rostrum to the telson provides a consistent index of somatic progress, and the value of 1.3 centimeters [Lp = 1.3 centimeters] aligns with values reported for other members of the genus Orconectes that occupy similar thermal regimes. This size at maturity implies that many individuals spend roughly one to two years in an immature phase before entering the breeding population.

Neonates of Orconectes neglectus emerge from eggs with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0056 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0056 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of 2.2 millimeters. This diminutive starting mass reflects the relatively small yolk reserves packaged into each egg, which nonetheless sustain the newly hatched young through the initial days of yolk depletion before exogenous feeding begins. The wet weight at birth of 0.0056 grams [Wwb = 0.0056 grams] positions the ringed crayfish among species that produce moderately sized offspring for their clade, balancing fecundity against per-offspring investment. Berried females carrying embryos near hatching exhibit egg masses that corroborate this estimate closely, confirming the reliability of the diameter-based calculation under field conditions.

As individuals approach their asymptotic body size, they achieve an ultimate wet weight of 4.4 grams [Wwi = 4.4 grams], which represents the maximum body mass recorded for adults in established populations. This value is derived from the length-mass scaling relationship fitted to local collections and is consistent with the carapace length of 2.1 centimeters. The wet weight at puberty reaches approximately 0.913 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.913 grams], indicating that females attain reproductive capability at roughly one-fifth of their ultimate mass, a pattern typical of many cambarid crayfishes that allocate resources to early maturation. The disparity between pubertal and ultimate mass reflects continued somatic growth after the onset of reproduction, with molting intervals lengthening as the upper size boundary is neared.

Longevity records for Orconectes neglectus, maintained at a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], indicate a life span of approximately 1460 days [am = approximately 1460 days], which translates to roughly four years under these controlled thermal conditions. This lifespan estimate, drawn from observations of the related species Orconectes limosus, is thought to apply broadly within the genus for populations experiencing similar temperature regimes. The value of approximately 1460 days [am = approximately 1460 days] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] suggests that the ringed crayfish is relatively short-lived compared to some larger decapods, with mortality accelerating after the third year as senescence and molting-related risks increase.
